newsitem.title: USA: US SWAP SPREAD MOVEMENTS CONFINED TO AUCTION BLIPS.
newsitem.headline: US SWAP SPREAD MOVEMENTS CONFINED TO AUCTION BLIPS.

text.p: U.S. interest rate swap spreads were little changed on the week apart from technical blips linked to the Treasury's refunding, traders said on Thursday.
For instance, the three-year spreads widened nominally earlier in the week and then came back in after Tuesday's auction of the new three-year notes, they said.
"What happened was, the market widened out versus the old three-year because everyone was trading the new W.I.s (the new notes on a when-issued basis)," said a securities firm trader.
"When the W.I. came in, since that one has a higher yield because of its liquidity premium, the spreads came back in."

The three-year spread was bid at 28 basis points and offered at 29 bps on Thursday after widening as far as 30-1/2 bps bid and 32 bps offered early in the week. It had traded at slightly below 30 late last week.
"I think the same thing is going to happen with the 30-year," the trader added. "I think it will settle back down a couple of basis points lower."
The U.S. Treasury auctioned some $16 billion of three-year notes on Tuesday, $12 billion of 10-year notes on Wednesday and $10 billion of 30-year bonds today. The new issues settle on August 15.
Otherwise, traders said, trading had been relatively calm this week, despite a downturn in the underlying fixed income market since last Friday.
A swaps broker said most of the activity was in the front end, with ordinary two-way interest.
"It's just dealers trading positions," he said.

The 10-, 12-year area maintained a bid-tone due to perceived longer-term scarcity of Treasuries. The 10-year spread was pegged at 40-1/2 bps bid, 41-1/2 bps offered, half a point wider from late last week.
But traders said activity in the longer end had generally been subdued.

"Because the (interest rate) market's going up, a lot of the new issues coming out have not been swapped," the securities firm trader said. "Corporations are content to pay fixed while the market's moving up.

"When they think the market's topping out, they'll probably swap then and they'll get much better Libor minus whatever," he added. "And they'll roll the profit from that trade into a new swap (eventually)."
